https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmr.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Police used tear gas to disperse hundreds of protesters who took to the streets on Monday over prolonged power cuts By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Thomas Naadi Published 9 hours ago The Gambia's President Adama Barrow has urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts, saying the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa. His comments follow protests on Monday night in the capital Banjul and surrounding areas over blackouts that residents say have sometimes lasted up to 48 hours. "When you lie down in the heat and the dark, believe that you are not alone in that darkness," Barrow said, pledging to boost power supplies by next month. The Gambia supplements its own generation with imported electricity, including supplies from Guinea and neighbouring Senegal. The tiny West African country has endured persistent blackouts since June, with outages becoming longer and more frequent during the current hot season as soaring temperatures drive up electricity demand. Frustration boiled over on Monday night, when protesters took to the streets in Banjul and surrounding areas, burning tyres and blocking roads over the prolonged power cuts. Police used tear gas to disperse crowds in Westfield area as they moved towards the headquarters of the national electricity company, Nawec, with some chanting. "Barrow must go". Protesters also gathered outside the vice-president's residence in Farato, where banners at an office of Barrow's ruling National People's Party were damaged. The unrest comes just months before a presidential election expected in December, in which Barrow is seeking a controversial third term. In a televised address on Tuesday night, Barrow acknowledged the hardship caused by the blackouts but warned protesters against damaging public infrastructure, saying it would only worsen the disruption and divert money towards repairs. "Let us not destroy in a moment of anger what we suffered so long to gain," he said. The president admitted there had been shortcomings in the government's planning, power generation and maintenance systems, calling the resulting outages "a national security issue" and an "emergency". "I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night," the president, promising that supplies would improve by the end of October. He said a new 24-megawatt generating unit was being installed at the Brikama power station and would be commissioned by the end of next month. A contract has also been awarded for a 50MW solar power plant in Soma, although no completion date was given. "For a system of our size, this is considerable power, enough to make a big difference in your homes," Barrow added. The president visited facilities for the national energy utility on Tuesday morning and promised that The Gambia would receive new generators this week. Gallo Saidy, the Nawec chief, also appealed for patience, saying reduced electricity imports from the regional grid had contributed to the shortages. He said lower rainfall this year had reduced the electricity available through the regional network. "We are aware of the frustration and constraints that the Gambian people have," he said. "We are just asking The Gambian people to give us a little bit of time and patience." Nawec had warned in August that unusually high temperatures had driven a surge in electricity demand, while a technical problem had also affected a major generating unit supplying imported power. A Fidesz szombat kora délután reagált a feljelentésre, a volt miniszterelnök titkársága által kiadott közleményben rágalmazásnak nevezték a vádakat, és azt írták, „Koncz Zsófia a legkiválóbb államtitkárok egyike volt, aki mindent megtett azért, hogy a magyar családok a lehető legtöbb segítséget kapják gyermekeik felneveléséhez. Koncz államtitkár asszony a saját választókerületében is rendezvényeket tartott és támogatott a Családbarát Magyarország Program keretében. Jól tette. A miniszter viszont ezt bűncselekménynek nevezi.” Az ellenzéki párt szerint miniszter jobban tenné, ha inkább a program folytatásáról döntene. Photograph: PA Labour Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest Caroline Davies Wed 21 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public. Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS. At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him. However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved. “In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.” Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.” MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.” He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”. Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party. In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928. Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney. The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died. Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937. While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public. One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.” Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files. MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war. The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained. A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”. However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.
